opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest mistake is treating signals and systems as a box you check before getting to the "real" robotics. For me it's actually the language underneath almost everything a robot does. When you're tuning a controller, filtering IMU data, thinking about why a learned policy oscillates on hardware but looked fine in simulation, you're really asking signals-and-systems questions: what's the bandwidth, where's the delay, what frequencies am I amplifying?

So my advice is to study it with a robot in mind from day one. Don't just compute Fourier transforms on paper. Take real sensor data, an encoder or an accelerometer from a cheap board, and look at its spectrum. See the noise, see the vibration from the motors, then design a filter and watch what it does to your phase and your latency. That moment when you realize your beautiful low-pass filter just added enough delay to destabilize your loop teaches you more than a whole problem set.

Second, keep both the continuous and discrete views in your head. Physics is continuous, but your robot runs at 500 Hz or 1 kHz on a computer. Sampling, aliasing, zero-order hold: these aren't academic details. Plenty of real bugs come from a control rate that's too low or a sensor that isn't anti-aliased.

Third, connect it to the modern tools. A lot of students now go straight to reinforcement learning or large models, and that's great, but these ideas still show up there. Action smoothness, control frequency, why policies with action chunking behave differently, why a system identification step helps sim-to-real transfer: all of that becomes much clearer if you understand linear systems, frequency response, and stability intuitively.

And finally, aim for intuition over formalism. You should be able to look at a Bode plot or a step response and *feel* what the robot is going to do. The math matters, but the goal is that when something shakes or lags on the real hardware, your first instinct is "where's the pole, where's the delay," rather than just retraining or randomly tuning gains.

r001.rationale: It recommends practical, robot-centered intuition and applications, but does not contrast connecting the subject to fundamental mathematics with learning every Kalman-filter derivation.

r002.rationale: It discusses spectra, frequency response, and filtering, but does not characterize signal processing as superposition in the frequency domain.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I get this question a lot from students, and my honest answer is that most of them are studying signals and systems backwards.

The typical path is: take the course, memorize the Fourier transform tables, learn to draw Bode plots, pass the exam, and then forget all of it until a robot starts oscillating in the lab and you have no idea why. The theory was never connected to anything physical, so it never stuck.

So my first piece of advice is to start from a real signal as early as you can. Get an IMU, a motor encoder, a microphone, anything that produces a stream of numbers. Log it. Plot it. Look at the noise. Then ask the simple questions: what frequencies are in here? What happens if I average it? Why does my derivative estimate look like garbage? Once you have felt those problems with your own data, concepts like sampling, aliasing, and filtering stop being abstract. They become answers to questions you already have.

The second thing is to treat the discrete-time side as the main event, not the appendix. In a classical course, continuous-time theory comes first and the discrete case is squeezed in at the end. But every robot you will ever build runs on a sampled loop at some fixed rate. The z-transform, discrete filters, latency from sampling and computation, those are the things that will bite you. I would almost rather a student deeply understand what a one-sample delay does to a control loop than be able to derive Laplace transforms by hand.

Third, learn to think in terms of frequency content even when you are not doing formal analysis. When you look at a control problem, you should instinctively ask what bandwidth you need, where the noise lives, and where the structural resonances are. That intuition is what signals and systems really gives you, and it carries into estimation, perception, and even learning-based methods. A lot of what people call tuning is really just reasoning about frequency without saying the word.

And finally, do not skip the math, but do it in the right order. Read the derivation after you have seen the phenomenon, not before. The math then feels like it is explaining something rather than being inflicted on you.

If I had to compress it: build something that moves, watch it misbehave, and let that pull you into the theory. The students who come out strongest are not the ones who did the most problem sets. They are the ones who can look at a shaky trajectory and immediately say, that is a filtering problem, or that is a sampling problem, and know what to try next.

r001.rationale: The response encourages connecting theory to physical robotics signals and learning the math after observing phenomena, but it does not mention the Kalman filter or state the criterion’s comparison with deriving it.

r002.rationale: The response emphasizes reasoning about frequency content, bandwidth, noise, and resonance, but it does not characterize signal processing as superposition in the frequency domain.

astra-6.text:
I would encourage students to connect the math to a physical system as early as possible. Signals and systems can feel abstract when you’re just looking at equations. But if you have a motor, you give it a command, and you measure how it moves, suddenly those equations are describing something you can see.

Start with the fundamentals: how we represent a signal, how a system responds to an input, and what changes when you look in the frequency domain. Then do small experiments. Change the input, change the sampling rate, add a filter, and compare what you predicted with what actually happened. Why is there a delay? Why does the output oscillate? Why does filtering make the measurement smoother but the response slower?

That connection is especially useful in robotics, because sensing, computation, and control all interact. You want to develop enough intuition to look at a robot’s behavior and ask a good question about what’s happening. The math gives you a way to answer it.

r001.rationale: It prioritizes connecting the fundamentals of signals and systems to physical robotics experiments and intuition; it does not focus on deriving a particular filter.

r002.rationale: It mentions examining signals in the frequency domain, but does not characterize signal processing as superposition there.

sol-6.1.text:
I would encourage students to connect the math to a physical system as early as possible. Take a motor, give it an input, measure its response, and try to build a model. Then the ideas in signals and systems—frequency response, stability, filtering—become tools for answering questions you actually care about.

For robotics, it’s especially useful to understand what happens between sensing and acting. Your measurements are noisy, your controller runs at a finite rate, and there’s always some delay. What does that do to the behavior of the robot? Can you filter the noise without introducing too much lag?

So learn the theory carefully, but keep going back and forth between equations, simulation, and experiments. When your model predicts one thing and the hardware does something else, figuring out why is a very valuable part of learning.

r001.rationale: The response encourages connecting theory and math to physical systems, but it does not prioritize fundamental mathematics over teaching Kalman filter derivations.

r002.rationale: It mentions frequency response, but does not characterize signal processing as superposition in the frequency domain.
